title: Exfiltration
summary: Exfiltration is the unauthorised transfer of data from an environment the organisation controls to a destination it does not, and it is usually the point at which an intrusion becomes a reportable breach. The activity normally follows a recognisable sequence: locating and collecting data of value, staging it on an intermediate system, reducing its size or obscuring its content through compression and encryption, splitting it into transferable chunks, and moving it over a channel that is likely to be permitted. Channel choice is a trade-off between volume and stealth. Large transfers over ordinary web or file-sharing protocols are fast but visible; low-and-slow transfers over DNS, commodity cloud storage or a long-lived command-and-control channel are quieter but take longer and depend on the destination remaining available. Defences fail most often at the egress boundary, where broad allow-lists for web traffic, personal cloud storage and remote access tools make almost any destination reachable. Detection combines data-side and network-side evidence: unusually large or oddly timed transfers, access to repositories the account does not normally touch, new external destinations, protocol use that does not match the port, and anomalous DNS query volumes or label lengths. Mitigations that work are egress filtering with explicit allow-lists, data classification with controls that follow the data, scoped credentials that limit what a single identity can read, and monitoring of cloud storage and collaboration platforms rather than only the corporate perimeter.
objectives: You will be able to describe the collect, stage, compress and transfer sequence and the evidence each step creates.
You will be able to compare common exfiltration channels by volume, stealth and detectability.
You will be able to evaluate egress controls and explain why permissive allow-lists undermine them.
You will be able to use flow, DNS and cloud audit telemetry to build exfiltration detections.
You will be able to prioritise data classification and credential scoping as exfiltration mitigations.
